title: 1 Kings 14:21–31
context: The narrative turns to Judah, where Rehoboam, Solomon's son, reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem. Under him Judah also falls into idolatry, building high places, pillars, and Asherah poles, and adopting the abominations of the nations. In his fifth year Shishak of Egypt plunders the temple and palace, carrying off Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze. War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continues throughout his reign. Second Chronicles 12 adds that Judah humbled itself and was spared complete destruction.

verses.text: Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, "the city which the LORD had chosen." His mother is Naamah the Ammonitess. Arminian readers note that God's choice of Jerusalem gives Rehoboam privilege and responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God keeps his promise to preserve a lamp for David in Jerusalem (11:36). The mention of Naamah may hint at the foreign influences Solomon allowed, though the text does not explain it.

verses.text: Judah did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins which they committed, above all that their fathers had done.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah does evil and provokes the LORD to jealousy "above all that their fathers had done." Arminian readers note that Judah, despite the temple and David's line, freely follows the same path as Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's covenant language of jealousy reflects his exclusive claim on his people. Judah's privileges do not protect it from sin, and its guilt is all the greater.

verses.text: For they also built for themselves high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
verses.arminianNotes: They build high places, pillars, and Asherah poles "on every high hill and under every green tree." Arminian readers see widespread idolatry, the people choosing the practices God had forbidden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrasing echoes warnings in the law and prophets. Judah's worship has become indistinguishable from that of the nations God drove out.

verses.text: There were also sodomites in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations which the LORD drove out before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: "There were also sodomites in the land." The Hebrew term is often understood as cult prostitutes connected with pagan worship (compare Deuteronomy 23:17). Arminian readers see covenant life corrupted by pagan practice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse links Judah's practices to "the abominations of the nations which the LORD drove out." The land God cleansed is being defiled again by his own people.

verses.text: In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak of Egypt comes against Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that 2 Chronicles 12:2 attributes the invasion to Judah's unfaithfulness, a consequence of their choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God uses a foreign king to discipline his people. Second Chronicles 12 adds that the princes humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous," and God limited the judgment.

verses.text: and he took away the treasures of the LORD’s house and the treasures of the king’s house. He even took away all of it, including all the gold shields which Solomon had made.
verses.arminianNotes: Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields. Arminian readers see the loss of Solomon's glory within a few years, a warning about how quickly blessings can be squandered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wealth God gave Solomon is stripped away in one generation. Outward splendor cannot protect a people who have turned from God.

verses.text: King Rehoboam made shields of bronze in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the guard, who guarded the door of the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam replaces the gold shields with bronze. Arminian readers see the substitution as a picture of a kingdom keeping up appearances while its true glory has faded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the poignant contrast between gold and bronze. Many see a symbol of diminished glory, as Judah carries on its rituals with lesser substitutes for what God had given.

verses.text: It was so, that as often as the king went into the LORD’s house, the guard bore them, and brought them back into the guard room.
verses.arminianNotes: The guards bring out the bronze shields whenever the king goes to the LORD's house. Arminian readers note that the ceremony continues, though its splendor is gone, a picture of religion going through the motions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Rehoboam maintains the outward forms of royal worship. Ceremony continues, but the narrative has already shown the idolatry beneath it.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Rehoboam's acts are written in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note that the narrator again focuses on the king's faithfulness rather than his political achievements.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Kings selects material to show how each king stood before God. The fuller record exists elsewhere, but the inspired account gives the verdict that matters.

verses.text: There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
verses.arminianNotes: "There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually." Arminian readers see the ongoing division of God's people as the fruit of sin on both sides, with tragic consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the division God decreed (12:24) continues as constant conflict. The once-united people of God live in hostility, a sign of the cost of unfaithfulness.

verses.text: Rehoboam slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess. Abijam his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam dies and is buried in David's city; Abijam succeeds him. Arminian readers note that the mention of his Ammonite mother is repeated, perhaps to underline the influences that shaped his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that despite Rehoboam's failures, David's line continues on the throne in Jerusalem. God keeps his promise to David even through unfaithful heirs.
